assumptions.summary: Crossroad and toll delays are omitted and road-condition delay is ignored.
Traffic counts and chosen roads remain fixed after the intervention.
Lane changing is omitted because recognition, prediction and fleet turnover are considered immature.
All vehicles share a four-meter length, regular width and homogeneous class behavior.
Autonomous vehicles communicate and react quickly enough to need no human safety interval.
Both traffic directions are combined because they are assumed not to disrupt each other.
A one-second response time and a seven-cell-per-second maximum represent human and road timing.
Uniform daily arrivals and randomized initial speed represent the basic no-peak case.
A normalized dual-Gaussian curve represents morning and evening traffic peaks.
Dedicated lanes bar autonomous cars from common lanes and human cars from reserved lanes.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Four named Seattle-area highways in four counties define the road-network scope.
Daily section traffic count, lane count, road length and 224-section membership feed the simulator.
Four-meter cells, a one-second clock, seven-cell maximum speed and one-second response are fixed.
Autonomous share enters equations 13-14 and initial speed is randomized from zero to 60 miles per hour.
The basic experiment runs all 224 sections for one hour and repeats each condition 100 times.
The time model runs 24 hours for 224 sections and repeats each condition 20 times.
The peak comparison uses 17:00 and emphasizes 0, 10, 50 and 90 percent autonomous share.
Busy-hour, peak-average and daily-average velocity curves support the tipping comparison.
The lane counterfactual reserves two direction-specific lanes and compares average and busy roads.

dependency_graph.handoff: Cited density-speed behavior motivates speed as an output but does not define the final evaluator.
Class-dependent safe intervals feed the movement branches.
Cell geometry and state receive generated vehicles and support movement.
Cell occupancy and completions feed passing time, velocity and variance criteria.
Dual-Gaussian hourly density replaces uniform arrivals in the time-based run.
Basic cellular trajectories feed autonomous-share comparisons.
Velocity and two variances supply network scenario metrics.
Peak timing defines the 17:00 and peak-hour comparisons.
The same movement model is rerun after lane-access changes.
Average velocity and space variance compare lane policies.
Network share results provide the no-dedication baseline.
Adverse lane results identify new lane-count and route-response scenarios for later network runs.

independent_extensions.summary: Fit density-speed regime domains and continuity to held-out detector data.
Replace reaction-only spacing with calibrated braking, leader-deceleration, latency and communication-failure dynamics.
Test cell length and time step jointly and publish collision/state invariants for simultaneous updates.
Separate served throughput, queues, travel time and two variances; define equilibrium without reciprocal singularity.
Fit arrivals by direction and time, specify entry blocking and release seeds plus run-level uncertainty.
Release dual-Gaussian observations, parameters, objective, residuals and out-of-sample fit.
Validate road geometry, aggregation and color maps against independent section-speed observations.
Estimate the tipping point with a changepoint rule, bootstrap interval and adjacent share grid.
Vary reserved-lane count and access flexibility with infrastructure cost, enforcement, equity and reversal rules.
Couple adjacent sections through conserved junction states and add class-dependent lane and route choice.

An easy instantaneous output is rejected and rebuilt into a traceable network evaluator.

language_observations.summary: Reusable human writing moves center on benefit narrowing, limitation-backed omission, easy-observable rejection, mirrored criteria, internal baseline failure, disclosed display strategy, metric-separated sensitivity, local threshold scope, adverse unfinished repair, weakness-to-interface translation and time-limit candor.
one simulator is extended through three operating regimes: Make baseline, time enrichment and intervention dependencies visible before mechanics.
the official letter opens with concrete congestion consequences: Give a public decision practical stakes before proposing technology.
four broad benefits are narrowed to one modeled job: Expose why one capability is relevant and the others are out of scope.
technology limitations justify omitting lane changes: Tie a simplification to a real recognition or maturity constraint.
a physical contrast precedes a named quantity and equation: Let the reader see the safety interval before formalizing it.
cellular state is introduced one component at a time: Make each geometry, state and clock choice inspectable.
an accessible instantaneous output is replaced by a decision metric: Show why a convenient raw value is insufficient.
occupancy counts recover passing time and average velocity: Narrate a multi-equation evaluator as a sequence of observable transformations.
time and space criteria are defined with mirrored prose: Teach why two variances answer different stability questions.
the problem order is mirrored by three simulations: Keep simplification, regime repair and policy test aligned to task parts.
the transition rule is narrated before the flowchart: Make collision, gap and class branches readable before code.
the repeat count appears beside horizon and domain: State what was rerun and why at the point of use.
velocity and variance receive different sensitivity judgments: Preserve disagreement between metrics instead of averaging it away.
a sparse baseline is called unrepresentative before the route changes: Let an internal failure trigger the time-based model.
the visualization changes when the analytical target changes: Tell the reader which changing point the new display is meant to reveal.
road abstraction and color meaning precede the network reading: Make a schematic network plot interpretable before drawing a conclusion.
the tipping point is restricted to busy roads at peak time: Bind an approximate visual threshold to its operating regime.
time and space variance figures are interpreted together: Use a reference line and preserve two operating implications.
dedicated lanes are implemented as access constraints: Describe an intervention as exact input and transition changes.
a high-share decline leads to a mechanism and an unrun repair: Preserve adverse evidence and say why the next branch was not simulated.
extensibility is explained through a replaceable input or rule: Make a strength concrete by naming the extension point.
each admitted weakness is translated into a model interface: Turn criticism into an implementable next state or handoff.
different information by vehicle class motivates route choice: Derive a future module from an actor-level information difference.
unfinished work is openly attributed to time: Keep an implementation gap visible without abandoning its analytical value.
the conclusion retains benefit, crossover and overload boundaries: Compress several operating decisions without erasing reversals.
delay variance is translated into less buffer time: Connect a technical stability output to a stakeholder consequence.
transition prose, flowchart and code close the implementation loop: Let the reader trace a rule across three representations.

results_trace.summary: Average velocity rises steadily with autonomous share, but the full-range change is only about 1 m/s or four percent.
Space velocity variance falls by about 66 percent, so variance is much more share-sensitive than speed.
At 50 percent autonomous share, the peak network map is visually more uniform and the source reports nearly unhindered flow.
Only busy-road sections at peak time show a visible tipping point, near 45 percent.
Time variance falls most near the 45-percent region and peak-hour space effects become less significant around 50 percent.
Without dedicated lanes, average and busy-road performance are better below roughly 68 percent autonomous share.
With two reserved lanes, performance becomes slightly better above roughly 68 percent.
At about 95 percent or more, too few reserved lanes crowd autonomous vehicles and performance declines or flattens.
The Conclusion carries 45-, 68- and 95-percent operating boundaries into the policy summary.

source.title: Self-driving vehicle's prospect in traffic network

source_quality.summary: All 29 physical pages were read and visually reviewed. The paper narrows a benefit set to congestion, builds cellular criteria before experiments, lets a sparse baseline trigger a dual-Gaussian repair, preserves different speed/variance sensitivity, scopes a busy-peak tipping point, exposes dedicated-lane harm and translates source weaknesses into next-model interfaces.

decisions: which autonomous capability enters the cellular model, which behaviors are omitted, how performance is constructed, when a uniform baseline is insufficient, where a share threshold appears, and when reserved lanes harm or help
inputs: cell size, lane count, road length and daily traffic count

title: Self-driving vehicle's prospect in traffic network
unresolved_questions: The three density-speed regimes lack stated domains, continuity conditions and empirical calibration.
The no-safety-interval premise overstates sensing and synchronization and omits braking, latency, failure and road condition.
Crossroads and toll delays are removed despite the network decision context.
Fixed traffic counts suppress route and demand response to changed travel times.
No lane changing conflicts with the dedicated-lane policy and merge-heavy network.
Identical four-meter vehicles omit trucks, buses and heterogeneous performance.
Combining both directions assumes symmetric, noninteracting demand.
Reaction distance alone omits braking distance and leader deceleration.
The four-meter grid, seven-cell speed ceiling and one-second clock have no discretization sensitivity.
The occupancy-derived speed is called capacity without served demand, throughput, censoring or spillback.
Reciprocal variance can diverge near zero and is called equilibrium without a stability definition.
Uniform independent arrival probabilities omit empirical arrival fit and entry blocking.
The source code can generate an initial speed of eight although the stated maximum is seven.
The transition rule has no simultaneous-update, collision-resolution or invariant specification.
One hundred repeats lack seeds, run-level variance and confidence intervals.
Four-percent and sixty-six-percent sensitivity judgments use endpoint changes without uncertainty.
Dual-Gaussian parameters, fitting data, criterion and goodness-of-fit are absent.
Hourly parameter adjustment conflicts with the claim of second-level density precision.
The schematic road geometry and color scale are not validated against held-out detector speeds.
The forty-five-percent tipping point is selected visually without a changepoint rule or uncertainty.
The sixty-eight-percent dedicated-lane crossover is visually interpolated from one allocation and one model.
Autonomous cars are barred from common lanes, a restrictive assumption that drives the lane comparison.
The ninety-five-percent decline motivates more lanes, but that repair is explicitly untested.
Infrastructure cost, enforcement, induced demand, equity and transition logistics are absent.
Claimed exactness from one-second updates is unsupported by grid or clock comparison.
Claimed stability is unsupported by reported run-level statistics.
Independent segment simulation breaks junction conservation; the source admits count loss or gain.
Route choice is omitted even though automation changes information and travel time.
The Conclusion presents approximate visual thresholds more firmly than the analysis warrants.
The Governor letter's 1.5-2-times claim is not reconciled with the roughly four-percent full-day velocity change.
Safety, fuel and emergency-response benefits appear in the letter without being simulator outputs.
MATLAB appendices are fragments without inputs, environment, seeds, tests, outputs or a runnable package.

writing_logic.summary: shared cellular representation -> uniform baseline -> dual-Gaussian time extension -> dedicated-lane branch -> velocity evaluator -> conditional decision
local congestion -> delay/accident/emergency consequences -> no-new-lane objective -> autonomous intervention
named roads -> 10/50/90 shares -> equilibria -> tipping point -> dedicated-lane condition -> government suggestions
four potential benefits -> select fewer traffic jams -> shorter spacing mechanism
lane-marker and prediction defects -> fleet-turnover concern -> omit lane changing
human/autonomous diagram -> safe-interval definition -> equation -> class-specific action
cell length -> lanes -> gap -> section length -> speed -> response -> traffic count
instantaneous speed is accessible but insufficient -> occupancy sum -> passing time -> average velocity
on one hand time variation -> on the other hand space variation -> paired equilibrium criteria
first ignore peaks -> secondly add daily peak distribution -> lastly add dedicated lanes
conflict -> safe gap -> vehicle class -> acceleration/deceleration/synchronization -> repeat 100 times
about four-percent speed change -> insensitive; about sixty-six-percent variance change -> sensitive
two daily peaks -> dual-Gaussian function -> hourly adjustment -> 20 repeated full-day runs
changed analytical target -> changed visualization strategy -> stress the changing point

sections -> map blocks -> road direction/length -> color meaning -> network judgment
